unit.title: Use strategies to identify job opportunities

summary: This unit teaches you how to find and win work in hotels, villas and other tourism businesses. You will learn to know your own skills and goals, find out where jobs are advertised and where they are not, read a job advert, spot job scams, write a CV and cover letter, contact employers, do well at an interview, and keep a job search going with a plan and a log.

blocks.p: Getting trained is only half of getting a job. The other half is finding the jobs, showing an employer that you are the right person, and not giving up when the first reply is no. This unit teaches that second half. It is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees who are getting ready to work, and it is useful again every time you want a better job.

Most people look for work by luck: they wait, they ask one cousin, they send one CV. A trainee who uses **strategies** does better. A strategy is a plan with steps: know what you offer, look in many places, apply carefully, follow up, and learn from each reply.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Know yourself and set career goals
List your skills, interests, values and needs
Write a SMART goal for your job search and your career
Know the usual career steps in a hotel or villa
Find job opportunities
Use adverts, employer websites, the Centre, HEART/NSTA Trust, government services, licensed agencies and job fairs
Use people you know and send CVs to employers who have not advertised
Find out which jobs are in demand
Stay safe from job scams
Spot the warning signs
Check agencies and overseas offers through official sources
Read job adverts
Pick out duties, essential and desirable requirements, closing date and how to apply
Decide honestly whether to apply
Apply properly
Get your documents ready
Write a CV and cover letter matched to the job
Choose referees and keep your online image respectful
Contact employers and attend interviews
Make a polite enquiry by phone, email or in person
Prepare for, take part in and follow up an interview, including by video call
Plan and track your search
Make a job search plan and keep a log
Follow up, handle rejection and check job offers before you accept

flow: Know yourself and set a goal
Find out where the jobs are
Read adverts and choose
Prepare documents, CV and letter
Apply or enquire
Interview
Follow up and record
Accept, or learn and keep going

blocks.note: How you are assessed: a theory paper with multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays, and two group practical tasks in the Centre. In the practicals you analyse real or sample job adverts, check an advert for scam signs, make a job search log and a SMART plan, write a CV and cover letter, practise a phone enquiry, and take a mock interview. Use made-up details if you do not want to share real ones.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Never put your real passwords, bank details or home address on any practice form or in any photo you hand in. Your safety online is part of the job search.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Before you look at a single advert, find out what you have to offer and what you want. Employers will ask, and the answers also stop you applying for jobs that do not suit you.

head: Look at
What it means
Hospitality examples
rows: Technical (job-specific) skills
Skills for one kind of job, learnt in training or on the job.
Making up a bed to standard
Cleaning a bathroom with the right chemicals
Setting a table
Using a floor machine safely
Transferable skills
Skills useful in nearly every job, so you can carry them from one workplace to another.
Communicating with guests and co-workers
Teamwork
Being on time
Solving problems
Staying calm when it is busy
Interests
What you enjoy doing.
Meeting guests at the front desk or the restaurant
Working behind the scenes in housekeeping, laundry or the kitchen
Working outdoors at an attraction
Values
What matters most to you in a job.
Fair pay
Learning and promotion
A friendly team
Time with family
Needs and limits
Facts about your life that affect which jobs you can take.
Shifts, weekends and public holidays
How you travel and how far
Family duties
Whether you would work overseas

ul: Write your lists down. Ask your instructor and classmates what you do well: others often see strengths you miss.
Also list the skills you still need, such as a first aid certificate or a second language. These become your training goals.
Be honest. An honest list helps you pick jobs you can do well and explain your strengths at interview.
A needs and limits list is not a weakness. If you cannot work late because of your family or transport, look for day shifts and tell employers early, not after you are hired.

blocks.p: A **SWOT** has four boxes. **Strengths** and **weaknesses** are about you. **Opportunities** and **threats** come from outside you.

head: Box
Example for a trainee room attendant
rows: Strengths
Reliable, neat, trained to standard, speaks some Spanish
Weaknesses
No work experience yet; nervous at interviews
Opportunities
New hotel opening nearby; Centre job fair next month
Threats
Many applicants for each job; bus fares are high

blocks.p: A vague goal such as 'get a good job' gives you nothing to do on Monday morning. A **SMART** goal does.

head: Letter
Means
Example
rows: S
Specific: says exactly what you want
A room attendant job at a villa or hotel in Negril or Lucea
M
Measurable: you can count it
Send CVs to six places and attend at least two interviews
A
Achievable: you can really do it
Six applications in four weeks, not sixty
R
Relevant: it fits your qualification and life
Day-shift housekeeping, near your home
T
Time-bound: it has a date
By 30 November

blocks.note: A goal for the next four weeks is a short-term goal. 'Be a housekeeping supervisor in five years' is a long-term goal. Short-term goals are the steps that lead to the long-term one.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Write a **plan** under the goal: each step, its date, and what you need (copies of certificates, a phone credit, a lift to the interview). Look at it every week and change it when something is not working.

sections.title: Careers and where the jobs are

blocks.p: Hospitality has many departments, and each has its own ladder. If you know the ladder, you can see where an entry job could lead and what to learn next.

head: Department
Usual steps up (entry to senior)
What helps you move up
rows: Housekeeping
Room attendant, public area or laundry attendant; senior room attendant or floor supervisor; housekeeping supervisor; assistant executive housekeeper; executive housekeeper
Reliable work to standard
Learning every task
Supervision training and NVQ-J Level 3
Kitchen
Kitchen porter or kitchen assistant; commis chef; chef de partie (section cook); sous chef; head or executive chef
Food safety certificates
Learning each section
Cookery qualifications
Front office
Front desk agent or reservations agent; front desk supervisor; assistant front office manager; front office manager
Computer skills
Languages
Guest service training
Food and beverage
Server or bar assistant; senior server or bartender; supervisor or head waiter; restaurant or bar manager
Product knowledge
Mixology and service training
Leading a team
Villa
Villa attendant or housekeeper; villa cook or butler; villa manager
Cooking, guest care and organising skills
Dealing with owners and guests

blocks.p: Job titles differ from one property to another, so ask what each title means where you are applying. In a small villa one person may do several of these jobs. A larger hotel has more steps.

ul: Do excellent, reliable work. Supervisors remember who is on time and who needs no reminders.
Learn every task in your department, and then ask for more responsibility.
Keep training: Level 3, supervision, first aid, computers, a second language such as Spanish or French.
Tell your supervisor about your goals and apply when promotions are announced.
To find out what a job such as concierge is really like, talk to someone who does it. This is called an **informational interview**: you ask about the work, not for a job.

Most hotel and villa jobs are in the **resort areas**: Negril, Montego Bay, Ocho Rios, Runaway Bay, Port Antonio, the south coast around Treasure Beach and Kingston's hotels. Some jobs are in attractions, restaurants, tour companies, transport and guest houses.

Jamaica's **high season** runs roughly from December to April. Many properties take on extra staff before it starts. These **seasonal jobs** may end when the season ends, but they give experience and contacts, and good workers are often kept on.
Look at where you can realistically live and travel. A job that costs most of your pay in transport is not a good job for you.

Up-to-date **labour market** information (reports on which jobs are growing or short of workers) is published by government and training agencies. Use it, not guesses or old newspapers, to decide which skills to build.

blocks.note: Other ways to use your skills: start a small business (for example, catering, cleaning services or guest-house help). Working for yourself is **self-employment**. It needs a plan, money and registration, so learn about it in your entrepreneurship studies first.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Do not look in one place. Use several sources every week. Some jobs are advertised; many are not.

head: Source
How to use it
Take care
rows: Newspaper and online job adverts
Check often. Apply before the closing date.
Read the whole advert. Check the employer is real.
Employer websites and social media pages
Follow hotels, villa companies, restaurants and attractions you would like to work for. Many post vacancies there first.
Use their official page, not a copy.
The Centre's career or job placement office and job board
Ask about openings and for help with your CV.
It helps you; it cannot promise you a job.
HEART/NSTA Trust and government employment services
Ask about job listings, placement and approved overseas work programmes through the Ministry of Labour and Social Security.
Use the official offices and websites only.
Licensed recruitment agencies
They match workers to employers.
Check that the agency is licensed. A real agency does not ask you to pay to be given a job.
Job fairs and recruitment days
Many employers in one place. Dress smartly and bring several copies of your CV.
Bring your own pen; fill the forms yourself.
People you know
Tell family, friends, instructors, church members and former co-workers what job you want.
Be polite and thank people.
Work experience and volunteering
Placements, community events and charity work build skills, references and contacts.
Treat them like a real job: be on time and reliable.
Sending your CV with a short letter
Write to properties you like, even with no advert, asking about openings.
Address a named person where you can.

blocks.p: Many jobs, especially in small villas and guest houses, are filled by word of mouth before they are advertised. This is the **hidden job market**. You reach it by **networking**: making and keeping contacts with people who might hear of work. An owner who needs a helper often asks a neighbour or her cook first.

ul: Tell people what you are trained in and what job you want. One clear sentence is better than 'I need work'.
Ask them to tell you if they hear of an opening and, if they work in a hotel, whether they could pass on your CV.
At open days, job fairs and community events, introduce yourself politely to staff and managers, say what you are trained in, ask about work there, and note their contact details.
Never push, beg or ask for a job on the spot. Keep in touch without pestering, say thank you, and help others when you can.

blocks.p: An **elevator pitch** is a short spoken summary of who you are and what you offer. It is ready for any chance meeting. Example: 'Good morning. I am Shanice Brown. I have just finished NVQ-J Level 2 in villa services and I did my work experience at a hotel in Negril. I am reliable, I work to standard, and I am looking for a room attendant job. May I leave my CV?'

blocks.note: Use only the Centre's computers, or your own phone if your instructor agrees. Never enter personal details, passwords or bank details on a site during practice tasks.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Staying safe: job scams and overseas offers

blocks.p: Some people pretend to offer jobs so they can take your money or your personal details. Hotel work abroad is a common trap, because many Jamaicans would like to work overseas. A **job scam** takes your money, your documents or your identity.

head: Warning sign
Why it should worry you
rows: You must pay a fee for the job, a visa, training or 'processing' before you are hired
A real employer pays you. It does not charge you to start work.
The pay is far too high for the work
It is bait to make you act without thinking.
No interview, or an offer on the same day
Real employers check who they hire.
Pressure: 'only a few places left, pay today'
Scammers do not want you to stop and check.
Messages from a personal email address or only through social media
A real company has an address, phone number and website you can check.
Poor spelling and no company details
Real employers proofread.
Requests for your passport, bank details or TRN before a real offer
These can be used to steal from you.

flow: Do not pay and do not send documents
Research the company: address, phone number, website
Phone the number you found yourself, not the one in the message
Check any agency is licensed with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security
Talk to your instructor or family
Report scams to the police and warn others

ul: Get information about overseas work only from the **Ministry of Labour and Social Security** and its official programmes, or from well-known employers you have checked.
Never borrow money to pay a fee for a job. You may lose it all.
Do not click links in suspicious messages. Show them to your instructor.
A genuine overseas programme will have official forms, official offices and no private bank transfers to an individual.

blocks.note: If you have already paid or sent your passport, tell your family and report it to the police at once. Contact your bank if you gave bank details. The sooner you act, the more can be done. It is not your fault; scammers are clever.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: An advert tells you almost everything you need. Read all of it, slowly, more than once, before you decide to apply.

head: Part of the advert
What to check
rows: Job title, employer and place
Is it a real business? Can you travel there? Does the title match what you want?
Duties
What will you actually do each day?
Requirements: **essential**
What you MUST have to be considered, for example NVQ-J Level 2, a Food Handler's Permit, or the ability to work weekends.
Requirements: **desirable**
A plus, but not a must: for example a second language or a first aid certificate.
Hours, shifts and pay
Are the hours possible for you? Is pay shown? If not, ask politely later.
Closing date
The last day applications are accepted. Late applications are usually not read.
How to apply
By email, online form or in person; what to send; whom to address.

ul: Apply if you have all the **essential** requirements, or nearly all and can say how you will get the rest soon.
Do not apply if you lack something essential that you cannot get, such as a licence the law requires.
Do not make up skills you do not have. You will be found out, and it can cost you the job.
Follow the instructions exactly. If the advert says 'email only, no phone calls', send an email and do not call.

blocks.p: In your practical you fill in an analysis sheet for each advert. Include: job title, employer, location, duties, essential and desirable requirements, closing date, how to apply, and whether the job matches your skills. Also check the advert for scam warning signs.

blocks.note: An advert for a room attendant at a hotel in Ocho Rios may ask for NVQ-J Level 2 in housekeeping and a Food Handler's Permit as essential, with experience and a second language as desirable. Underline each requirement and tick the ones you meet.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Applying: documents, CV and cover letter

ul: **Identification and tax numbers**: your Taxpayer Registration Number (**TRN**) and your National Insurance Scheme (**NIS**) number. Many employers also ask for your NHT number and a government photo ID. Your birth certificate may be needed.

**Certificates and permits**: your NVQ-J certificate, other training certificates, and permits such as a Food Handler's Permit, which you get from the public health department after the checks it requires. Ask what your job needs.
**Police record or other checks**: some employers, especially those with guests in their homes, ask for a police record. Ask the employer what it needs and how long it takes to get.
**Passport-size photos** if asked.
Keep **copies** of everything in a folder, and the originals safe at home. Take copies to interviews and job fairs, and show the originals only when asked.

blocks.p: A **CV** (curriculum vitae) is a short, clear summary of you. It should be one or two pages, typed in a plain font, neat, with no spelling mistakes.

head: Section
What to put
rows: Contact details
Full name, phone number, a professional email address and the area where you live. (No need for your full address.)
Profile
Two or three lines: who you are and what job you want. For example: 'Trained room attendant with NVQ-J Level 2, friendly and reliable, seeking a housekeeping position in a resort.'
Education and training
Most recent first: qualifications, short courses, permits.
Work experience
Jobs, work attachments, part-time jobs and volunteering: employer, dates, main duties.
Key skills
Skills that match the job: making beds to standard, customer service, teamwork, languages.
Referees
Two people, with their permission.

ul: **Change your CV for each job.** Move the skills that match the advert to the top. Never invent skills.
Use an email address made from your own name, such as a.brown@ followed by your email service. Not a nickname.
Ask someone to proofread it. Save it as a PDF if you can, so the layout does not change on another computer.

blocks.p: A **referee** is a person who agrees to tell an employer about your work and character: an instructor, a work experience supervisor or a former employer. **Always ask permission first.** Tell them which job you are applying for and thank them. Do not use relatives as your only referees.
A **cover letter** is a short letter or email that goes with your CV. It names the job, says why you want it and how your skills match, and asks for an interview.

flow: Greet a named person, or 'Dear Sir or Madam'
Name the job you are applying for
Say why you want it
Show two or three matches with the advert
Say what is attached
Ask for an interview and say thank you

ul: Employers may look at your social media. Remove posts, photos and comments that are rude, drunken or unkind.
Set your accounts so that only friends see private posts.
Never post about a guest, a co-worker or an employer. Do not complain about a job online.

flow: Greet them and give your name
Say why you are calling
Give one short sentence about what you offer
Ask your clear question
Write down the answer and the name of the person
Thank them

ul: Phone in working hours, from a quiet place, with a pen ready. Do not ask about pay first.
Speak clearly and slowly, and do not chew or eat.
If the manager is busy, ask when to call again or for an email address to send your CV.
Find out about the property: where it is, what guests it serves, what it is known for.
Read the advert again and think how your skills match the duties.
Practise answers to common questions. Use real examples from your training, work experience, school, church or community work, and be honest.
Prepare two questions to ask, such as: 'What training do new staff receive?'
Get your documents ready and plan your journey so that you arrive **10 to 15 minutes early**.

head: Common question
What the employer wants to know
How to answer
rows: Tell me about yourself
Whether you suit the job
A short answer about your training, skills and what you want: not your life story
Why do you want to work here?
Whether you are keen and have done your homework
Mention something real about the property, and what you can offer
How would you deal with an unhappy guest?
Your attitude and judgement
Listen, apologise, solve what you can, report the rest to the supervisor
Tell me about a time you worked in a team
Teamwork
A real example, with what you did and the result
Can you work weekends and holidays?
Whether you can meet the shift pattern
Be honest; hotels work every day
Do you have any questions?
Whether you are interested
Ask about training, the team or the next steps, not holidays or leaving early

ul: Dress neatly and simply, be well groomed, and switch your phone to silent.
Greet everyone politely, shake hands if one is offered, sit up straight, make eye contact and smile.
Listen to the whole question, then answer clearly and honestly. Never speak badly of a past employer.
At the end, thank the interviewer.
Test your phone or computer, camera, sound and internet beforehand. Charge the device.
Choose a quiet place with the light in front of you and a plain background.
Dress as you would for an in-person interview. Log on a few minutes early.
Look at the camera when you speak. Keep your camera on.
Send a **short thank-you message** the same day or the next day.
If you are not offered the job, ask politely for feedback and keep applying. Use the feedback to improve your CV and answers.
Do not phone every hour, and do not tell people you got the job until you are sure.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, a good interview answer is respectful and clear. Use 'Sir' or 'Madam' or the person's title and surname unless they ask you to use their first name.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Planning and keeping your search going

blocks.p: A job search can take weeks or months. A plan and a log keep you moving and keep you from missing closing dates.

head: Column
Example
rows: Date applied
12 November
Employer and job
A villa company in Negril, villa attendant
How you applied
Email with CV and cover letter
Contact person
Mrs Campbell, HR
Closing date
30 November
Follow-up date
19 November
Result and notes
Called on 19 November; interview on Friday at 10 a.m.

ol: Week 1: update your CV; make copies of certificates and permits; tell your contacts you are looking.
Week 2: ask two people to be referees; set up your log; check job sites, newspapers and employer pages; apply for your first jobs.
Weeks 3 and 4: apply for at least three suitable jobs a week; follow up on those from week 2; practise interview answers with a classmate.
End of the month: review. What worked? What will you change?

ul: If you hear nothing after one to two weeks (or by the date in the advert), phone or email politely to check that your application was received. Say your name, the job and the date you applied.
Do not turn up unannounced, phone repeatedly, or post angry comments on the business's page.
Many people apply for each job. A no does not mean you are not good enough.
Thank the employer, ask for feedback, and ask if they will keep your CV for other openings.
Keep a routine, rest, exercise and talk to people who support you.
While you search, keep learning, volunteer, or take short-term work. It builds skills, references and contacts.
Get the offer in writing: job title, duties, pay, hours and shifts, start date, probation period and who you report to.
Check pay against the national minimum wage and ask about normal deductions: statutory deductions such as NIS, NHT, education tax and income tax appear on your payslip.
If you do not understand something, ask. Do not accept in a hurry.
Tell other employers politely when you have accepted a job, and thank everyone who helped you.

blocks.note: Later in your career, a Level 3 qualification can open better-paid and more senior jobs. Keep your certificates safe and your CV up to date.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: I can list my technical and transferable skills, interests, values and needs.
I can write a SMART job goal and a four-week plan with dates.
I can describe the usual career steps in housekeeping, the kitchen, front office, food and beverage and a villa.
I can explain why many jobs are seasonal and where the hotel and villa jobs are.
I can name at least five sources of job opportunities and say how to use each.
I can explain the hidden job market and how to network politely.
I can give a 30-second pitch.
I can spot the warning signs of a job scam and say how to check an overseas offer.
I can read an advert and tell essential from desirable requirements, the closing date and how to apply.
I can get my documents ready: TRN, NIS number, certificates, permits and copies.
I can write a CV and cover letter matched to a job, and choose referees with their permission.
I can make a phone enquiry politely and clearly.
I can prepare for, behave at and follow up an interview, including a video interview.
I can keep a job search log and follow up on applications.
I can deal with rejection and check a job offer before I accept it.

terms: A skill for a particular job, such as making a bed to standard.
A skill useful in many jobs, such as communication or teamwork.
A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
The usual steps up from an entry job to a senior job.
A job available only at certain times of the year, such as the winter tourist season.
Facts on which jobs are in demand, and where.
Jobs filled through contacts and word of mouth, never advertised.
Making and keeping contacts who might help you hear about jobs.
A short spoken summary of who you are and what you offer.
A meeting to ask someone about their job and career, not for a job.
An event where many employers meet job seekers in one place.
An agency with official permission to match workers with employers.
A fake job offer that aims to get your money or personal details.
Something you must have to be considered for a job.
A plus, but not a must.
Taxpayer Registration Number; National Insurance Scheme number.
Curriculum vitae: a short summary of your education, experience and skills.
A short letter or email that goes with your CV and asks for an interview.
A person who agrees to tell an employer about your work and character.
A record of each application, follow-up and result.
A short period of work done to gain experience during or after training.
Working for yourself instead of an employer.

c1.title: Shanice finishes her course in Lucea
c1.text: Shanice Brown, 19, has just completed her NVQ-J Level 2 in Hanover. She wants a hotel or villa job in Negril or Lucea. Her notes list: making up a bed to standard, speaking basic Spanish, staying calm when rushed, and using the vacuum cleaner and trolley. She must be home by 6 p.m. to care for her younger brother, and she travels by route taxi because her family has no car.

c2.title: A room attendant advert in Runaway Bay
c2.text: A villa company in Runaway Bay advertises for a room attendant. Essential: NVQ-J Level 2 in housekeeping (or six months' experience) and the ability to work weekends and public holidays. Desirable: a first aid certificate and a driver's licence. How to apply: email a CV and cover letter to the HR address by 21 November. 'No phone calls, please.' Kerrian has the NVQ-J Level 2 and a clean, neat CV, but no first aid certificate. He goes to church on Sunday mornings and would rather not work then.

c3.title: A message about work in Canada
c3.text: Tamika receives a WhatsApp message from 'Canada Hotel Jobs Jamaica'. It says: 'Hotel jobs in Canada, US$25 an hour, no interview needed. Send J$45,000 as a processing fee and a photo of your passport today, only five places left.' The message has several spelling mistakes and gives no company address or phone number. Her friend Kayon says she has already paid.

c4.title: A video interview for a villa job
c4.text: Ricardo has an interview for a villa assistant job with a villa company in Port Antonio. It is by video call on Thursday at 10 a.m. He has never had a paid job, but he did four weeks of work experience at a guest house and helps at his church's youth events. He shares a small room with his brothers, and the Wi-Fi sometimes drops.

c5.title: Marlon's job search
c5.text: Over three weeks, Marlon has applied to eight hotels and villas by email and in person. He has no written record. When a hotel manager phones back, he cannot remember which job she is calling about or whom he spoke to. A villa company has not replied after ten days. A hotel in Ocho Rios writes that the position has been filled.

questions.q: Which skill on Shanice's list is a transferable skill rather than a technical skill?
o: Staying calm when she is rushed
Making up a bed to the hotel standard
Using the vacuum cleaner and the trolley
Mixing a cleaning chemical correctly
questions.why: A transferable skill is useful in almost every job. Staying calm helps in housekeeping, the kitchen or the front desk. The other skills are technical skills that belong to particular jobs.

questions.q: Shanice must be home by 6 p.m. and travels by route taxi. How should this shape her job search?
o: Treat it as a need, and look for day-shift jobs within easy travel
Keep it from employers, and arrange a way around it after she is hired
Leave it out of her planning, and apply for every job that she sees advertised
Apply only to jobs overseas, where working hours are not a problem for families
questions.why: Needs and limits are part of knowing yourself. Looking for jobs that fit them, and telling employers early, avoids taking a job you cannot keep.

questions.q: Which goal is a SMART goal for Shanice's job search?
o: By 30 November, apply to six properties and attend two interviews
Find a nice job near home as soon as the right chance comes up for her
Work hard at my search, and get a hotel job at some time in the future
Apply to as many hotels as possible, and keep going until one of them says yes
questions.why: This goal says what, how many and by when, and it is possible to do. The others have no number, no date, or no clear target, so Shanice could not tell if she had reached them.

questions.q: Kerrian has no first aid certificate. What does the advert mean for his application?
o: It is desirable only, so he can still apply and say he is willing to train
It is essential, so an application without it will not be considered at all
It is needed only after he is hired, so he should not mention it in his letter
It is needed only by supervisors, so it does not apply to a room attendant
questions.why: The advert lists first aid under desirable requirements: a plus, not a must. He can apply, show that he meets the essential ones, and mention that he would like to train.

questions.q: Kerrian would prefer not to work Sunday mornings. What is the most honest and sensible decision?
o: Weekends are essential here, so he should look for a job that suits him better
Apply and say he is available for any shift, then ask for Sundays off once he starts
Apply, and ask the employer to change the weekend rule to suit his church plans
Apply, and phone the employer afterwards to complain about the weekend requirement
questions.why: Hotels and villas work every day, and weekends are an essential requirement here. Agreeing and then refusing breaks trust. Honest planning means choosing jobs whose shifts you can actually work.

questions.q: The advert says 'No phone calls, please.' Kerrian has a question about the uniform. What should he do?
o: Follow the instruction: apply by email and put the question there
Phone the manager anyway, because his question is different from the others
Go to the villa in person, to show how keen he is to work for them
Ask a friend who works there to phone the HR office on his behalf
questions.why: Following instructions exactly is the first test of a good employee. A short, polite question in his email respects the rule. Ignoring it, or sending a friend, can get an application set aside.

questions.q: What should Kerrian's cover letter do?
o: Name the job, show how his training fits the duties, and ask for an interview
Repeat his whole CV line by line, so the employer need not open the attachment
List the pay and days off he expects, so the employer knows his terms at once
Explain why he left school, and describe how difficult his life has been lately
questions.why: A cover letter is short and aimed at one job. It links your skills to the duties in the advert and asks for the next step. Pay demands and long life stories do not help you at this stage.

questions.q: Which feature of the message is the biggest warning sign?
o: It asks for money and a passport photo before any real offer
It arrives by WhatsApp, which is a poor way to send a job offer
It mentions a job in Canada, where hotels do not hire from Jamaica
It states the pay in US dollars, though Jamaican jobs pay in J$
questions.why: Real employers pay you; they do not charge a fee to start work. Asking for money and identity documents first, with pressure to act today, is the clearest mark of a scam. The other features alone do not prove a scam.

questions.q: What should Tamika do first?
o: Pay nothing, and check the offer with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security
Pay half of the fee now to hold a place, and check the offer when she has the rest of the money
Ask Kayon for a copy of her receipt, and pay the same way if the receipt looks real
Send the passport photo only, since the message asked for the fee as well as the photo
questions.why: Never pay or send documents before checking. The Ministry runs the official overseas work programmes and can say if an offer or agency is genuine. Talking it over with a trusted adult is also wise.

questions.q: Kayon has already paid the fee and sent her passport photo. What is the best advice for her?
o: Tell her family, report it to the police, and warn her bank if she gave details
Wait a few weeks to see if the job arrives, since the company may simply be slow
Send the sender a polite message asking for the fee to be paid back to her
Post the message online and ask other people to pay so that the fee is refunded
questions.why: The sooner a scam is reported, the more can be done. Waiting or negotiating with scammers gives them time. Kayon should also protect her accounts and warn others.

questions.q: How should Ricardo prepare for the video interview?
o: Test the device, find a quiet spot, dress neatly and log on early
Log on exactly at 10 a.m. and sort out the camera while the interviewer waits
Join from the bus stop so that he does not lose time travelling to the villa
Keep the camera off to save data, and answer by speaking only, without being seen
questions.why: A video interview is a real interview. Testing the equipment, a quiet place and neat dress show care. Joining early leaves time to fix a problem. A camera that stays off hides your body language.

questions.q: The interviewer asks: 'Tell me about a time you helped a guest.' Ricardo has no paid job. What is the best answer?
o: Give a true example from his work experience at the guest house
Make up a story about a famous guest he once served at a large hotel
Say that he has never had the chance to help anybody in that way
Say that he is willing to learn, and that he has no examples to give
questions.why: Interviewers want real examples, and work experience, school, church or community help all count. Inventing a story is dishonest and easy to catch, and saying nothing wastes a chance to show what you can do.

questions.q: At the end, the interviewer asks if he has any questions. Which is the best one for Ricardo to ask?
o: What would a normal first week look like for a new villa assistant?
How many days can I take off during my first three months at the villa?
Will the villa pay for my bus fare to and from work every single day?
Can the villa lend me some money if I need it before my first payday?
questions.why: A question about the work shows you are interested in doing it well. Questions that are only about time off or money, asked first, can suggest you care more about benefits than the job.

questions.q: The video call drops two minutes into the interview. What should Ricardo do?
o: Reconnect at once, apologise briefly, and carry on calmly
Give up, since the interview is now certainly ruined for him
Wait an hour and then phone the company to ask for a brand new date
Send a long message blaming his internet company for the whole problem
questions.why: Technical problems happen, and employers notice how you handle them. Reconnecting quickly and staying calm shows maturity. Blaming others or giving up does not.

questions.q: What would have prevented Marlon's confusion when the manager phoned?
o: A job search log showing the employer, job, date and contact person
A longer CV that lists every hotel in Jamaica that he has ever visited
Saving the manager's number in his phone before he had applied there
Telling the manager he was not sure and asking her to phone back later
questions.why: A log records where you applied, whom you spoke to and when to follow up. It also keeps closing dates from being missed and helps you sound organised on the phone.

questions.q: The villa company has not replied after ten days. What should Marlon do?
o: Politely phone or email to check his application arrived, and note it in his log
Call every day until someone gives him a clear answer about his application
Go to the villa and wait there until the manager is free to see him in person
Stop applying to villa companies, since this one has clearly decided against him
questions.why: A polite follow-up after a week or two shows interest and checks that the application was not lost. Repeated calls or turning up unannounced can lose you the job.

questions.q: The Ocho Rios hotel writes that the position has been filled. What is the most helpful reply?
o: Thank them, and ask whether they will keep his CV for future openings
Reply that he is disappointed, and that they chose the wrong person for it
Ask the hotel to give him the name of the person that they have hired
Say nothing at all, since a reply to a rejection is only a waste of time
questions.why: A polite reply keeps the door open. Many hotels keep good CVs for later vacancies, and your professional manner may be remembered. Complaining or asking who was hired does you no good.

questions.q: A villa owner in Treasure Beach tells her neighbour that she needs a cook's helper and will ask around before putting up an advert. What does this show job seekers?
o: Many jobs are filled by word of mouth, so tell people what work you want
Jobs in villas are never advertised, so there is no point in reading adverts
Only neighbours are allowed to apply for jobs at small properties like hers
Villa owners only ever hire people who have already worked for them before
questions.why: This is the hidden job market. Telling family, neighbours and contacts clearly what job you want, and asking them to pass on your CV, puts you in line for jobs that never reach a newspaper.

questions.q: Bernard is offered a job at a resort from December to April. What kind of job is this, and what should he do?
o: A seasonal job: do it well, as good workers are often kept on
A permanent job: sign at once and stop looking for any other kind of work
A scam: refuse it, since real jobs never end on a fixed date in the year
A training job: expect no pay, since seasonal staff are always unpaid workers
questions.why: Seasonal jobs run with the tourist high season. They give experience, references and contacts, and reliable seasonal staff are often given other work or kept on when the season ends.

questions.q: Which shows the usual order of steps up in a hotel's front office, from entry level to senior?
o: Front desk agent, front desk supervisor, assistant manager, front office manager
Front office manager, front desk supervisor, front desk agent, then the general manager
Bell attendant, executive chef, front desk supervisor, then the housekeeping supervisor
Front desk agent, sous chef, assistant front office manager, executive housekeeper
questions.why: Each step adds responsibility for guests and for staff. Knowing the ladder helps you set goals, such as learning the reservations system or a language, to earn the next step.
